index.html.index.001: Firmware, or the present state of local reality. This handbook describes v3.0x. Its menu pages, clock colours and encoder tables belong to that firmware generation. Other generations may have developed opinions of their own.
index.html.index.002: For questions about an order, write to info@toern.live. If the handbook and the unit disagree, record the disagreement in an issue on GitHub. This gives the next revision something useful to feel embarrassed about.
index.html.index.003: TŒRN is a sampler and step sequencer: a small rectangle in which time has agreed to travel left to right. Voices stack upward on its RGB LED grid, which also serves as the display. Four rotary encoders let you draw, sculpt and arrange events with considerably less paperwork than the universe normally requires. A Micro SD card supplies eight sample lanes for drums and one-shots; a three-voice synth and two mono synths handle melodic matters. You can record directly on the device, should reality produce a noise worth keeping.
index.html.index.004: This handbook begins where the delivery ends. While waiting for your TŒRN, you can meet its simulator, which is unusually patient about being misunderstood. Begin with Your first beat in 1 minute, then read onward. USB-C provides power; the SD card chapter explains the card. Readers already on speaking terms with the machine can head for the screen index or menu map.
index.html.index.005: How to find your way through this part of the universe
index.html.index.006: The sidebar divides the expedition into three groups. This is fewer than most expeditions require, and considerably easier to find your way home from:
index.html.index.007: Get started — make a beat in a minute, then inspect the hardware, matrix and controls. Establishing what the objects are before operating them is a useful local custom.
index.html.index.008: Compose — sequencing, pages, advanced tools, samples, sound design, the audio path, recording and note detail. This is where the noises acquire intentions.
index.html.index.009: Operate — tempo and MIDI, song mode, saving and the full menu: the practicalities of sharing a studio with a small electronic personality. Includes the screen index and troubleshooting, for when introductions go poorly.
index.html.index.010: Where a display matters, the chapter shows it. Encoder tables provide one column per knob, a rare case in which the number of explanations matches the number of objects being explained. Destructive and easily missed gestures have callouts. Links lead to the menu map and screen index whenever a feature has acquired a page of its own.

first-beat.html.first-beat.001: Your first beat, before the universe adds conditions
first-beat.html.first-beat.002: There are people who buy a musical instrument, read its entire manual and then make their first sound. These people are an inspiration to us all, and must be stopped before they organise the cupboard. The following seven steps let a fresh-from-the-box TŒRN make a beat while your enthusiasm still has its shoes on. Allow about a minute. Reading the remarks will, admittedly, make it a longer minute.
first-beat.html.first-beat.003: First, permit there to be electricity.
first-beat.html.first-beat.004: Flip the side switch and let the boot animation finish. Machines like a small ceremony before work; people generally require coffee and a journey. You arrive in draw mode, looking at a mostly dark grid with dim coloured bands on rows 2–15. This is the instrument waiting for an idea. It is remarkably tactful about how long that can take. The bands are voice lanes; their addresses are in The matrix → voice lanes.
first-beat.html.first-beat.005: Find something with a definite opinion.
first-beat.html.first-beat.006: Turn encoder 1, the leftmost knob, to the red row. You have selected voice 1, the factory kick drum. Of all the available sounds, a kick is unusually comfortable announcing that something has begun. It needs no preamble, has little interest in harmony, and considers a second announcement after a short interval entirely appropriate. These are excellent qualifications for your first collaborator.
first-beat.html.first-beat.008: Turn encoder 4, the rightmost knob, to move the cursor along time. Short-press it to place a note. Put four notes on every fourth step: 1, 5, 9 and 13. Each light is a promise that a kick will happen there. Four regularly spaced promises make the familiar four-on-the-floor rhythm, which has supported a surprising amount of human happiness considering how little floor it specifies.
first-beat.html.first-beat.009: Ask time to honour the appointments.
first-beat.html.first-beat.010: Short-press encoder 3. A red vertical line travels left to right: the playhead, checking your promises in order. You should hear the kicks. At the end it goes round again. This is the first significant advantage over booking appointments in ordinary life, where repeating the same four events indefinitely tends to attract enquiries from the people involved.
first-beat.html.first-beat.012: Turn encoder 1 to another voice row and add notes on steps 5, 9 and 13. The new voice joins the kick without either of them needing to establish who started the band. Leave playback running while you place the notes and hear the arrangement change on its next visit. Already the silence has become something with a schedule. You are entitled to call this composition, even if you arrived here by wondering what that knob did.
first-beat.html.first-beat.014: Choose a voice with encoder 1 and tap touch 1, the left pad, to enter single mode. The grid tints in that voice’s colour and the rows now offer its pitches. Turn encoder 1 to choose a pitch and place a few notes; different rows should sound different. The kick’s colleagues have acquired upstairs rooms in which to be melodic. Tap touch 1 again to return to draw mode, where each voice resumes its own lane.
first-beat.html.first-beat.015: Stop, briefly, before becoming a career.
first-beat.html.first-beat.016: Press encoder 3 again to stop. You have made a beat with four knobs and a patch of lights. This is a perfectly respectable achievement; resist the urge to disqualify it because you now understand how it was done. Next, visit Hardware, Matrix and Controls. They explain the objects you have just been operating with the cheerful confidence of someone who has not yet read their job descriptions.

hardware.html.hardware.001: An inventory of the things with edges
hardware.html.hardware.002: A new instrument presents an appealing surface and several holes of uncertain significance. The owner’s first task is to distinguish the holes into which sound goes from those through which it escapes. Getting this right early saves a considerable amount of looking accusingly at cables. Here is TŒRN, surveyed from the outside inward.
hardware.html.hardware.003: Begin with the large luminous rectangle
hardware.html.hardware.004: The RGB LED grid occupies most of the face. It is the display, the musical landscape and, when necessary, a set of very small signs. Below it stand four RGB-lit rotary encoders, evenly spaced along the front strip. Between the grid and the encoders sit the circular capacitive pads touch 1 on the left and touch 2 on the right. Touch 3 lives on the right bottom edge. This is a sensible arrangement once you know it. Until then, it resembles a panel designed by someone who expected you to know it. Ports A–C (line out, USB-C, headphones) sit on the lower left edge, D–F (MIDI in, MIDI out, power) on the lower right, all below the matrix. Audio and recording points G–J run along the bottom; touch 3 is K at its right end.
hardware.html.hardware.005: The unit from above. The letters give its openings fixed addresses, a convenience the cables themselves have never thought to provide.
hardware.html.hardware.006: Line out — 6.35 mm stereo TRS, tip left and ring right, on the lower left edge below the matrix. Send this to a mixer or interface. Its level is independent: the audience need not share the precise volume at which you prefer to hear yourself thinking.
hardware.html.hardware.007: USB-C — lower left edge. Power, firmware updates, serial access and USB audio output to a computer all use this opening. You may know somebody at work who has accumulated a similar number of unrelated responsibilities. The socket appears to be coping rather better.
hardware.html.hardware.008: Headphone out — 6.35 mm (¼″) stereo TRS on the lower left edge, for headphones or in-ears. The level is adjustable. This provides a private venue in which an idea can become good before the rest of the room is invited to have views about it.
hardware.html.hardware.009: MIDI in (TRS) — lower right edge, Type-A TRS. Standard MIDI arrives from another device. The visiting machine can contribute notes and timing without having to explain its taste in either.
hardware.html.hardware.010: MIDI out (TRS) — lower right edge, Type-A TRS. Sends clock and notes. Now the other machine can discover what it is like to be told when things should happen.
hardware.html.hardware.011: Power switch — physical slide on the lower right edge. Turns the unit on and off. After the USB socket’s extensive list of duties, the switch’s commitment to a single subject is rather moving.
hardware.html.hardware.012: Internal mic — capsule on the bottom edge. The shortest route from an interesting sound in the room to an interesting sound that is your responsibility.
hardware.html.hardware.013: Micro SD slot — bottom edge; holds samples, kits, patterns and songs. Push to seat the card, push again to eject. Switch the unit off before inserting or ejecting. A card is a small object to hold this much of your musical life. Put it somewhere more considered than the pocket in which you also keep crumbs.
hardware.html.hardware.014: Mic in (6.35 mm) — external microphone input on the bottom edge, between the SD slot and line-in, with adjustable gain. A vocal mic and a synth cable can stay connected side by side. There is no requirement that the vocalist and synthesist get along equally well.
hardware.html.hardware.015: Line in — bottom edge, 6.35 mm stereo TRS, tip left and ring right. Connect a synth, drum machine or modular system. The current recording path takes only the left input and saves mono WAVs. If the wonderful bit lives entirely on the right channel, arrange for it to move before recording. Its wonderfulness will not persuade the left input to hear it.
hardware.html.hardware.016: Touch 3 — capacitive pad at the right end of the bottom edge. Press/hold on the grid for live/fast-rec, or hold in the sample browser to enter record mode. This is where a passing noise can be made to stay, long after everyone else has forgotten why somebody was hitting a mug with a spoon.
hardware.html.hardware.017: The controls and their working arrangements
hardware.html.hardware.018: Once the cables have found their holes, your hands need something to do. The physical controls in this overview fall into three families. Unlike most families, their disagreements can generally be settled by consulting the current screen:
hardware.html.hardware.019: Four RGB-lit rotary encoders, numbered 1–4 from left to right. Each turns, short-presses and long-presses. Their jobs change with the screen, while their positions remain reassuringly fixed. Row 1 displays small hints above them. This is the instrument’s concession to the fact that a person can remember where four knobs are or what they currently do, but may appreciate help doing both at once.
hardware.html.hardware.020: Three touch-sensitive pads on this hardware map: circular touch 1 and touch 2 between grid and encoders, plus touch 3 on the right bottom edge. Touch 1 toggles single mode; touch 2 opens the menu; both together open filters or the sample browser; touch 3 records. The combinations care which pad arrived first. See Controls → Touch pads for the firmware’s full touch repertoire and the consequences of being fractionally early.
hardware.html.hardware.021: Right-side power switch — physical on/off. Its job remains the same on every screen. We include this fact because constancy deserves recognition when it occurs.
hardware.html.hardware.022: The matrix is the entire display. There is no second screen waiting beneath a cover, and no bank of menu buttons you have overlooked. Notes, menus and editing controls all take turns occupying the same patch of light. This saves space on the panel and spends a little of it in the handbook. The matrix explains how to recognise which conversation you are having.
hardware.html.hardware.023: The occupants you cannot point at
hardware.html.hardware.024: Battery: internal LiPo. Makes it possible to move away from a power cable and experience the peculiar freedom of looking for somewhere else to sit.
hardware.html.hardware.025: Speaker: a small internal speaker. Sufficient to let the device demonstrate that it has an idea, though the idea may appreciate a larger room and a better sound system later.
hardware.html.hardware.026: Internal mic + Mic-in jack: built-in microphone and 6.35 mm external microphone input. One records the room conveniently; the other lets you be more particular about which bit of the room deserves a microphone. Both make the room a potential supplier of samples, which can change your attitude towards a squeaky chair.

matrix.html.matrix.001: A map of a place which keeps changing its mind
matrix.html.matrix.002: One of the reassuring things about a map is that the thing marked “river” will usually still be a river when you arrive. The TŒRN grid makes a more adventurous offer. The same lights can be notes, pitches, pages, menu text or controls, according to what you are doing. The river may have become a volume slider. Before setting off, establish which kind of landscape is currently being displayed. This chapter supplies the landmarks that stay useful even when the scenery changes profession.
matrix.html.matrix.003: The local arrangements for space and time
matrix.html.matrix.004: Time runs left to right, from column 1 to column 32. This is unusually obliging of time. Elsewhere it has a habit of disappearing while you search for a cable and reappearing all at once when somebody asks when you will be ready. Here, column 1 sounds first and column 32 last. Voices run upward. Row 2 carries voice 1, row 3 voice 2, and so on through row 15. The numbering is one row out because row 1 has been reserved for hints. Row 16, at the top, is reserved for pages. The sound-producing population has therefore been housed between two floors of administration.
matrix.html.matrix.005: A coordinate is a complete address. The firmware calls it (x, y) and counts both from 1. The bottom row is y=1; the top is y=16. When the handbook says “row 1,” it means the lowest visible row. You may disagree with counting upward, but the cursor will continue to live at the address you gave it.
matrix.html.matrix.006: Rows 2–15 are the voice lanes, between the beat guide on row 1 and the page strip on row 16. Consult the diagram whenever the administrative floors begin to look inviting.
matrix.html.matrix.007: Row 1 — a modest public service for lost musicians
matrix.html.matrix.008: Losing beat one is easy. Continuing to nod as though you know exactly where it is can occupy an entire performance. In Draw, the bottom row provides a 4/4 beat guide: dim markers at step 1 and every fourth step after it. They remain calmly visible while you reconsider which of those kicks was supposed to be the important one. Row 1 cannot hold notes. Start placing those on row 2. The guide’s contribution to the music is to remain beneath it, knowing where it is.
matrix.html.matrix.009: Move the cursor to row 16 and row 1 changes duties. The beat guide gives way to encoder hints for the page tools. This is your first indication that a gesture which was about one note may now affect something much larger. The instrument has put up the appropriate signs. Reading them remains a local responsibility. See Pages+More.
matrix.html.matrix.010: Row 16 — the view from the planning department
matrix.html.matrix.011: A page is a whole stretch of pattern, represented at the top by one small light. The page strip holds up to 8 such lights, a remarkably economical way to represent several minutes of wondering whether the bass should come in yet. With the cursor on row 16, the strip becomes the TOOL-LANE. The same hands which were placing individual notes are now equipped to operate on pages. It is rather like reaching the end of a pencil and discovering that the eraser can remove the street.
matrix.html.matrix.012:
With the cursor on row 16, the following tools are available:
  • Delete a page by unpainting its strip LED.
  • Copy and paste a page.
  • In single mode, clear the focused voice’s current edit page.
  • In single mode, generate a random, scale-aware fill for the focused voice.
  • In single mode, use note-shift to move that voice’s notes in time or across rows.
Row 1 shows the active tools. Return the cursor to a voice row to resume individual-note work. The ability to leave the planning department before acting on its ideas is one of the instrument’s more useful features.
matrix.html.matrix.013: A page light reports what is happening there. It makes no attempt to report whether what is happening there was a good idea.
matrix.html.matrix.015: Audible and being edited. Your attention and the music have arrived at the same address.
matrix.html.matrix.017: Audible. The music is here; your editing is elsewhere.
matrix.html.matrix.019: Being edited. Playback is elsewhere, or stopped. You have time to prepare a convincing explanation.
matrix.html.matrix.021: Contains notes. A visit will produce events.
matrix.html.matrix.023: Empty. The potential is extensive and the current obligations are few.
matrix.html.matrix.025: Beyond the active loop end. Playback turns back before reaching this slot, however patiently it waits.
matrix.html.matrix.026: Rows 2–15 — a residential directory with gaps
matrix.html.matrix.027: The directory is best read before trying to deliver a note. Voices 1–8 are samples, 11 is a three-voice poly synth, and 13–14 are mono synths. 9, 10 and 12 are unassigned. There is a row you can visit at each of those numbers, but no sound engine to answer the door. The hint and page strips are navigation and have no voices either. This leaves quite a lot of visible property which will never thank you for writing it a bassline. In DRAW, a voice appears one row above its channel number: voice 1 on row 2, for instance. In SINGLE, the building is reorganised around one tenant: rows become pitches of the selected voice. Upstairs now means higher pitch, instead of somebody else. A surprisingly large part of musical fluency consists of knowing which sort of upstairs you are dealing with.
matrix.html.matrix.028: Numbers are useful for identifying a voice to the firmware. Colours are useful for identifying it to someone who has spent the last ten minutes thinking “the purple one.” Each voice has a colour; below are the standard assignments in palette 0. You do not have to learn their names before making music. The purple one is a perfectly workable start.
matrix.html.matrix.029: The eight sample voices obtain their material from the SD card; Samples explains how to replace it. Voice 11 generates its own sound, with three-voice polyphony, ten presets and LFO/ARP. Voices 13 and 14 are independent mono synths with the same LFO and arpeggiator page. Positions 9, 10 and 12 contain no sound engine. Notes may be placed there, in much the same spirit that one may leave a chair out for a guest who has not been invited and does not exist. If silence is the result, the chair was not the problem.
matrix.html.matrix.030: For the musical route from oscillator through envelope, filter and effects, see Sound design. For the actual mixers and buses, see Audio path. One explains what is happening to the sound; the other helps find where it has gone. Both questions occur quite naturally during an evening spent following a cable behind a desk.
matrix.html.matrix.031: The cursor and the playhead, who are travelling separately
matrix.html.matrix.032: Two things may move on the grid while the music plays. This has caused perfectly sensible people to chase the wrong one with a knob. Establish which light belongs to you before trying to steer it:
matrix.html.matrix.033: The edit cursor marks where your next gesture will land. Encoder 4 moves it between columns; encoder 1 moves it between rows. A row-number helper can appear beside it. It is a pointer to your next decision, so it will quite happily remain over an empty cell while you consider a decision somewhere else entirely. Nothing has broken. You are thinking, and it has no instrument for detecting that.
matrix.html.matrix.034: The playhead is the red vertical line crossing left to right through the visible page. It sounds the current column. Notes brighten as they fire; muted lanes stay dark. Unlike the cursor, this line has a timetable. Trying to move it by turning the cursor knob will give you two moving things to worry about, which is a substantial increase over the original problem.
matrix.html.matrix.035: Stopped: only the cursor moves. Playing: the red playhead travels while the cursor stays wherever you left it. You may edit ahead of playback or behind it, or inspect one part while another is heard. Ordinary time is remarkably reluctant to permit this arrangement, which is one reason a small sequencer can be a more agreeable place to spend an evening than a large calendar.
matrix.html.matrix.036: Modes — please check what the room is for today
matrix.html.matrix.037: The grid’s meaning changes with its mode. You can remain in the same chair, holding the same instrument, and acquire an entirely different set of things to do. The two main sequencing views are explained in Sequencing:
matrix.html.matrix.038: Draw shows all voices at full intensity. The whole arrangement is available for inspection, including the notes you placed experimentally and have since become rather attached to denying.
matrix.html.matrix.039: Single brings one voice into focus and dims the others. A crowded piece of music can become a manageable question about a bassline. It is often kind to reduce a problem until it fits between two hands.
matrix.html.matrix.040: Other modes borrow the same grid for their own controls and information. Menu, for example, covers it with text and submenu dots while the music may keep playing underneath. The notes have not gone anywhere; your view has acquired a layer of business. Consult the Menu map to get through it. It is not necessary to finish all the business before returning to the music, a principle which deserves wider application.

controls.html.controls.002: A knob on an old radio could reasonably be expected to spend its life doing one thing. It turned the volume up, turned it down, and eventually became slightly scratchy about the whole business. These four knobs have entered a more flexible economy. Their duties depend on the screen, their rings advertise the current assignment, and you can ask them to turn, click or hold a thought. Once the arrangement is familiar it is very quick. Getting familiar is the part for which we have provided this chapter.
controls.html.controls.003: Meet the staff before changing their duties
controls.html.controls.004: The encoders are numbered 1–4, left to right. Each accepts a turn, a short press or a long press; certain commands require two held together. Their functions change between screens, but the knobs themselves stay in place. Learn that order first. It gives you four dependable landmarks in a system where the phrase “the one that changes the value” may apply, quite correctly, to all of them. The outlines below describe their usual work; the table for each screen gives the precise assignment.
controls.html.controls.005: Encoder 1: “Where?” The leftmost knob usually chooses the row, voice or lane. In L+R draw, a short press erases the note under the cursor; a long press with encoder 4 clears the page. It therefore has both the address book and access to demolition. Know whether you are turning it or pressing it.
controls.html.controls.006: Encoder 2: “What else?” Usually concerned with pages, row volume, the mute overlay or menu values. It handles much of the useful work which fails to fit neatly under “where,” “when” or “make a noise.” Organisations tend to give this work a small title and discover its importance when the person doing it goes away.
controls.html.controls.007: Encoder 3: “How does it sound?” Turn on the grid for fast filter; short-press to play or pause. Menus assign it other values. It lets you modify a sound, hear the result, and stop the result before deciding how you feel about it. Many creative discussions would benefit from a knob with this range of functions.
controls.html.controls.008: Encoder 4: “When?” The rightmost knob chooses columns in time and navigates menus. Short-press to write or toggle notes according to the draw setting, or to enter a menu page. Long-press over an existing note for per-step editing. The question “when?” can become quite detailed once velocity and probability join the conversation.
controls.html.controls.009: The RGB rings are the knobs’ current job descriptions. On a voice lane they take its colour; in filters they take the page tint; a binary toggle uses white. An unused knob goes dark. It has the rare good manners to look unemployed while it has nothing to do. Row 1 repeats the colours above the encoders, letting you glance between the panel and grid. Check these cues when a familiar gesture produces an unfamiliar result. The knob may have been reassigned while you were being certain about it.
controls.html.controls.010: Touch pads, and the importance of arriving first
controls.html.controls.011: The firmware listens to five touch pads. Touch 1 (L) and touch 2 (R) are between grid and knobs, beneath its left and right halves. Touch 3, on the right bottom edge, records. Touch 4 auditions the current voice. Outside TOUCHY, touch 5 acts as FN. L and R also recognise combinations, including the order in which contact begins. To your hands, touching both may feel like one event. To firmware it is a small historical record, with a first arrival and consequences. The table gives the relevant history:
controls.html.controls.013: Enter or leave single mode. One voice gets your full attention, a luxury seldom extended to members of an actual band.
controls.html.controls.014: Enter on voices 1–8, 11, 13 or 14. Row 16 and empty voice rows block entry. Once inside, exit from anywhere.
controls.html.controls.016: Open the menu. Playback can continue while the machine attends to your administrative visit.
controls.html.controls.017: From draw, single, paint or unpaint.
controls.html.controls.019: Open the sample browser for voices 1–8. This is the left-first combination.
controls.html.controls.020: Sample voices only. The synthesizers generate their sound and have no file to bring to the meeting.
controls.html.controls.022: Open filters on a voice supporting FX. This is the right-first combination.
controls.html.controls.023: Sample or synth voices, where the channel supports FX.
controls.html.controls.025: Next filter page. There is more to say about the sound, and another page on which to say it.
controls.html.controls.028: Turn left for backward sample playback (<<), right for forward (>>). The usual encoder value stays unchanged. A cymbal may now build towards the instant at which it was hit. You are under no obligation to explain this to the cymbal.
controls.html.controls.029: Sample voices 1–8, outside TOUCHY and sample capture. In TOUCHY, touch 5 plays voice 5 instead.
controls.html.controls.031: Hold in the sample browser for record mode. On the grid, press/hold for live/fast-rec; see Record → Live recording.
controls.html.controls.032: In the sample browser and on the grid.
controls.html.controls.033: FN modifies encoder input while held. Release it and normal turns, clicks and long presses return. While it is held in draw or single, encoder 2’s hint and ring turn pink. On the page row, FN + encoder 2 long writes a multi-voice page in draw, or rewrites the focused voice in single. The pink light is the instrument pointing at the knob that will do that.
controls.html.controls.034: Skin contact is sufficient. The pads measure capacitance. They do not measure determination, so additional pressure makes no more persuasive a request. A palm resting on the chassis can issue a touch while your fingers turn a knob. Keep your palms clear. Otherwise you will have two parts of your hand giving instructions, only one of which has read this paragraph.
controls.html.controls.035: Play, pause, and the button you were looking for
controls.html.controls.036: There is no separate play button. Its function lives in encoder 3: short-press on the grid to start, and press again to pause. The red playhead travels while running and vanishes when stopped. In filter mode, use encoder 3 long press instead. This lets you audition a change in the place where you are making it, rather than commuting between editor and grid with a steadily less accurate memory of what the last version sounded like.
controls.html.controls.037: Playback is global. Opening a menu to change BPM, MIDI settings or a pattern does not by itself suspend the loop. The instrument can play music while showing you something else. Once you get used to this, devices which insist on your undivided attention for a minor adjustment begin to seem rather demanding. You may carry out the business and return to the grid when ready; time has continued on the other side of the menu.
controls.html.controls.039: Some shortcuts and destructive commands require two encoders held at once. Both hands are thus invited to participate before a large quantity of notes disappears. This is a modest precaution. Human beings have a remarkable ability to carry out a mistake with both hands, but at least the mistake has had to make an appointment. The following gestures apply in draw and single mode; read the location as well as the buttons.
controls.html.controls.040: Page tools require the cursor on row 16 (y==16). Delete page, copy/paste, randomize, single-mode clear and note-shift belong to the page strip. On another row, the same fingers may issue a different command. Check the “Where” column before trying again. A correct gesture at the wrong address is an impressively precise way of doing something else.
controls.html.controls.042: Delete the page beneath the cursor by unpainting its strip LED. This clears its notes. The LED is a whole page represented very economically.
controls.html.controls.045: Clear the focused voice on the current edit page. Other voices retain their notes and any reservations they had about the arrangement.
controls.html.controls.048: Generate a scale-aware random fill for the focused voice. The machine supplies a suggestion; your part is deciding whether to look pleased.
controls.html.controls.051: Enter note-shift to move the focused voice’s notes. The notes keep their existence and acquire new addresses.
controls.html.controls.054: Open mute/solo while held; release to return. Encoder 3 changes fast filter; encoder 4 chooses a random sample.
controls.html.controls.057: Open the focused voice’s filters. You can investigate what the sound is doing from a position of useful proximity.
controls.html.controls.060: Toggle the note at the cursor. One press changes the answer to “is there a note here?”
controls.html.controls.063: Open the existing note’s per-step editor. A single event can have velocity, probability and conditions; brevity has never guaranteed a simple character.
controls.html.controls.066: Clear the current edit page: all voices in draw; focused voice only in single. There is no undo. Read the scope before involving your other hand.
controls.html.controls.069: Jump to BPM for tempo, clock source and brightness. Loudness is under VOL, where it can be addressed without changing the speed at which the problem arrives.
controls.html.controls.071: For a two-encoder command, bring both holds inside the long-press window. Release order does not matter. “Long-press encoder 1 together with encoder 4” means hold the two as a pair, rather than perform two separate long presses and hope the machine notices the theme. There is no prize for flourish. A calm, coordinated hold is sufficient; you may save the impressive fingerwork for the music.
controls.html.controls.072: Let go before 3 seconds and the boot continues, as if the hold had been a private rehearsal. At 3 seconds the matrix shows FULL / OK and the boot runs ETC → RSET → FULL, including the sample-card scan. Keep holding to 10 seconds and it shows RAM / OK after clearing the EEPROM. Let go during the RAM countdown and the wipe is skipped; FULL still runs.
controls.html.controls.073: Power-on only. Touch 2 has no startup hold.

troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.001: On the temporary failure of things to be reasonable
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.002: An instrument which has done exactly what you asked can look remarkably similar to one which has developed a fault. This is an awkward distinction to investigate while wearing headphones and feeling personally betrayed by a knob. Begin with the symptoms below. Most lead to a setting, a cable or an overlooked condition. The resets come later: powerful remedies with names short enough to leave out rather important details about your work.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.003: Which particular impossibility are we having?
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.004: Half the matrix is dark. I paid attention to both halves.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.005: The firmware is configured for a different arrangement of LED boards. It has no way of looking out through the lights to discover its mistake, so it continues displaying the wrong geometry with the confidence of a navigation system asking you to drive into a lake. Open ETC → ADV → LEDS and try 1, 1B, 2 and 2B until the display matches the hardware. The B variants flip the image for upside-down boards. This is an orientation correction; no soldering need follow merely because the picture looked alarming.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.006: My headphones have become exceptionally quiet furniture.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.007: Silence is easy to achieve and surprisingly difficult to locate. Start at VOL → MAIN: the level must be above 0. Then check VOL → GAIN: 1.0x is the old mix staging, while 0.0x mutes a bus. Check VOL → SPKR for speaker routing taking over, and seat the headphone plug fully. If line-out works and headphones still do not, inspect the TRS jack for a hardware fault. Following the signal in order is quicker than turning everything up, and much less exciting when the missing connection finally makes contact.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.008: The samples are on the card. The browser has an alternative account.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.009: The browser caches its file list. A cache is an excellent way to remember the world as it was, which becomes less excellent immediately after you improve the world. Run ETC → RSET → SD to rescan without changing patterns. Still absent? Check 16-bit mono WAV at 44.1 kHz and the layout in the SD card chapter. Calling a file “kick.wav” does not oblige its contents to be a compatible kick. Filenames have enjoyed this freedom from consequences for many years.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.010: The SD tool cannot find the port which is plainly right there.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.011: Use desktop Chrome or Edge at sdtool.toern.live. Android and Pixel browsers usually cannot see the Teensy USB serial port; physical proximity is insufficient to establish diplomatic relations. The card server answers from any screen. ETC → SD shows SCON: WAIT in yellow, then OK in green while a host is talking. Opening the port can reboot the Teensy; connect again after it comes back. Covered in SD card → SD tool.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.012: The machines agree on the tempo and disagree on “now.”
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.013: Use MIDI → SYNC. SYC> delays TOERN’s playback when it sends Play; SYC< delays its playback when it receives Play. Negative values add delay to the opposite path. Adjust in 1 ms steps and restart to hear the correction. A red -- means the selected value has no effect in the current mode. Settings persist.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.014: The BPM number is red. Should I look concerned as well?
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.015: The device is using EXT clock and the external timing is unstable or absent. It is waiting to be told when the next moment is, a reasonable service to expect of a clock master. Check that master’s cable and clock settings. To keep time internally instead, use BPM → encoder 3 and select INT. Red is useful information about the timing source. Becoming red yourself adds little to the diagnosis.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.016: I changed kits. My pattern appears to have changed its ambitions.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.017: The notes still trigger the same rows, but the rows now play different samples. Give the same score to a string quartet and four people carrying saucepans and some revision of expectations is inevitable. Select the old KIT number and short-press encoder 1 on the KIT screen to reload it. For future reference, save a PATT per KIT and note the matching KIT number. The rhythm is still yours; the cast was what changed.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.018: I cleared the wrong page. Surely there is an obscure remedy.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.019: There is no undo in RAM. Reload a previously saved PATT slot if available. Without a saved copy, the cleared work cannot be recovered. At this point a handbook is often expected to lower its voice and reveal the secret combination known only to engineers. There is no such combination. Save to PATT whenever an idea becomes worth keeping, especially just before deciding that a large part of it should disappear.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.020: The battery percentage seems to be writing an optimistic memoir.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.021: The percentage is an estimate from the charger IC. It has not stationed an accountant beside every electron. Treat it as a fuel gauge. Give it at least one complete cycle before trusting the curve: charge over USB until full, then run until shutdown. This lets the gauge encounter both “all of it” and “none of it,” useful reference points for an instrument whose main responsibility is describing everything in between.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.022: The touch pads are obeying an invisible musician.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.023: First inspect your palms. Capacitive pads accept skin contact without asking which part of you intended to be in charge. A hand can turn a knob and touch a pad at the same time while its owner remains sincerely convinced that only one thing happened. Lift your grip clear. If the problem continues in dry conditions, power-cycle to recalibrate the baseline. A ghost is a much less convenient explanation: there is no menu in which to change its settings.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.024: I turned slowly. The value went somewhere in a hurry.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.025: The I²C encoders can occasionally lose synchronisation. Power-cycle the unit. Reseating the SD card sometimes helps too; switch off before ejecting or reinserting it. Persistent jumping warrants a hardware investigation. There is a natural temptation to turn still more slowly, with the delicate concentration normally reserved for removing a splinter. An encoder which has lost synchronisation is unlikely to be impressed by your care.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.026: I asked for note detail and received a trail of notes.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.027: Encoder 4’s long press depends on context. Check SETT → DRAW: L+R also uses held encoder 4 for painting. Release any active paint gesture, then consult Note detail and start on an existing note. To enter single mode first, tap touch 1 on a valid voice. Repeating a gesture with greater conviction repeats the conditions which produced the first result. This is often mistaken for troubleshooting because it feels considerably more determined.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.028: Something is crossing the grid and I did not give it a job.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.029: A bright dot with a short trail bouncing through draw mode is usually MODE → PONG. PONG strikes and fires notes on muted voices only, leaving ordinary unmuted playback alone. Turn it OFF on that page or change its speed with encoder 2, 1–99. If instead two cartoon eyes appear after prolonged stopped inactivity, that is the separate idle animation. The machine has spent a while being looked at and is returning the courtesy. You need not make eye contact to resume work.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.030: I touched both pads. The sample browser did not consider this sufficient.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.031: It needs a sample voice, 1–8, and left pad first. A synth row goes to the filter editor: a synthesizer cannot show you the file it has never needed. Select a sample row with encoder 1, then try the left-first combination. Your hands may regard “both” as a complete description. The firmware would like to know who started it. On this occasion that detail is useful rather than tiresome.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.032: The notes were here before I improved their position.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.033: Note-shift saves continuously and commits positions on exit with encoder 4 short press. Check neighbouring pages. A shift can move a note beyond your current view without removing it from the pattern. This resembles the familiar process of putting an object somewhere sensible, followed by discovering that the present version of you has no access to the previous version’s reasoning. Here, at least, the search is limited to the pattern pages.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.034: Sample preview has started addressing the whole building.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.035: Lower VOL → PREV. To decide when preview happens, change VOL → PREV from ON to PRSS and audition with encoder 1, or choose SYNC to hear the sample on the voice’s pattern hits. This lets you browse without every candidate delivering a short public speech. There may be a very good sample in the folder. It is easier to recognise when the previous one has stopped shouting.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.036: ETC → RSET — read the demolition schedule
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.037: “Reset” sounds like putting a chair straight. Some of these options are closer to removing the room. There are seven distinct modes, with different things cleared and different things preserved. Encoder 3 selects; encoder 2 confirms. Read both columns before confirming. The machine will carry out the selected operation without first checking whether your expression corresponds to the consequences. That part of the interface is still supplied by you.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.042: Rescan the card, write samples/toern_wavs.txt for mute-mode random preview ?>, and invalidate the browser cache. SCAN, green checkmark, back to draw. This is a new catalogue of the shelves, with no rearrangement of their contents.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.043: Everything except the stale browsing/random index survives. Use after a card-reader swap or SD tool transfers.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.045: Restore filters, envelopes, synth parameters, octave helpers and audio effects to factory values across all voices. The notes keep their appointments; their tone returns to how it was before you began having ideas about it.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.046: Patterns and sample assignments survive. All tone settings return to factory values.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.048: Clear all notes, velocities and probabilities; set BPM to 100; reset volumes and filter data; delete and rewrite autosaved.txt; rescan the card. Read this as a list of operations. The reassuring brevity of FULL is a property of the label.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.049: The panel layout under ETC → ADV → LEDS (1 / 1B / 2 / 2B) and PATT-saved patterns survive. Almost nothing else in RAM does.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.051: Delete the saved pattern files 1–999.txt. These are the saved copies themselves. This operation removes a possible way back.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.052: autosaved.txt and the current RAM session survive.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.054: Delete kit folders except KIT 1. A very small word, “except,” is carrying the surviving collection here.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.057: Delete autosaved.txt and its .tmp and .bak recovery files, and clear the grid. This removes the autosave recovery copies as well as the main file.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.058: Settings, PATT slots and kits survive. The next boot is blank unless you pause-autosave again. For a damaged session, use FULL instead.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.059: No undo beyond reloading saved pattern files. FULL destroys unsaved RAM work. If you are considering whether a passage was good enough to save, save it before consulting the reset menu. Future you may have developed surprisingly generous taste.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.060: If it is still behaving like a difficult rectangle
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.061: Soft restart: switch off, wait five seconds, switch on. This ends most freezes. The wait is short enough to be tolerable and long enough to discourage pretending that a frantic flick of the switch counted as a fresh start.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.062: Reseat the SD card: power off, push to eject, reinsert firmly, then power on. This often resolves missing samples which survive a rescan. The card’s presence should be a mechanical fact, rather than a conclusion reached by looking at it from a hopeful angle.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.063: Reflash firmware: use USB-C and the Teensy 4.1 boot procedure. Reflashing leaves pattern files on the card intact unless you also reformat it. Reformatting is a separate operation. Two large buttons encountered in the same afternoon do not necessarily belong to the same cure.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.064: Persistent touch trouble: clean and dry the chassis, then reboot so the capacitive baselines recalibrate. Keep your palms clear during startup. Give the machine a chance to learn what “nobody touching it” looks like before supplying a demonstration of the opposite.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.065: For an encoder failure, dead LED or scratchy jack, inspect the hardware; the schematic and KiCad sources are in PCB/toern_revG/. Software can misunderstand a great deal, but no degree of improved understanding will close a broken connection. At this point the physical world must be invited back into the discussion.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.066: You may return to the noise you meant to make
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.067: If normal behaviour has resumed, take the opportunity to make music before either of you discovers another setting. The Screen index can identify an unfamiliar display. Save to PATT before switching off. Troubleshooting is satisfying when it ends, but the small act of saving is what lets a good evening remain a good evening when you turn the machine on tomorrow.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.068: Zeros every EEPROM byte, deletes settings.txt, shows RAM / OK, then restarts. The next boot writes factory settings. This is the stored memory of the instrument, not the pattern files.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.069: PATT files and kits on the card survive. The autosave still loads, so the current grid comes back. The panel layout returns to one panel. Saved settings do not survive.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.071: Hold touch 1 while switching on. Let go before 3 seconds and the boot continues. At 3 seconds the matrix shows FULL / OK: the boot then runs ETC → RSET → FULL, including the sample-card scan, and keeps the LED panel setting. Keep holding and a RAM countdown runs. At 10 seconds every EEPROM byte is cleared and the matrix shows RAM / OK; FULL still runs, so the panel layout returns to one panel. Let go during that countdown and the wipe is skipped. FULL still runs.

sequencing.html.sequencing.001: The practical advantages of having it happen again
sequencing.html.sequencing.002: A good noise is a pleasure. A good noise arriving at the right instant is music, or at least the beginning of a convincing argument that music is about to occur. A sequencer remembers those instants while you concern yourself with the noise. It also repeats them without becoming bored, asking for a break or suggesting that its contribution ought to be louder. This chapter covers draw, single and the L+R and R ways of placing and removing triggers. Larger operations have their own addresses: Pages+More for pages; Advanced Sequencing for mutes, note-shift, copy/paste and random generation.
sequencing.html.sequencing.004: Startup brings you to draw mode. Every voice is visible at full intensity, the red playhead crosses the rows together, and the edit cursor marks where your next gesture will land. The arrangement is spread out in front of you. A kick you placed confidently five minutes ago has become a small coloured fact amongst several other facts. You can now hear how they get along. This is where sequencing becomes more interesting than a list of instructions: the useful question stops being “which knob?” and becomes “what if that snare arrived a little later?” The knobs are there to let you find out.
sequencing.html.sequencing.005: Four voices on one page, with the playhead behind column 7. What looks like a pattern of lights is shortly going to make a number of quite definite claims about rhythm.
sequencing.html.sequencing.007: Choose the voice lane under the cursor. The colour identifies who will receive the next note.
sequencing.html.sequencing.009: Erase the note under the cursor. The lane stays unmuted; muting belongs to encoder 2. You have removed an appointment, rather than asked the voice to stop attending all of them.
sequencing.html.sequencing.011: Hold and turn to erase a trail. Long-press with encoder 4 to clear this page across all voices. The second operation deserves a pause before the second hand.
sequencing.html.sequencing.013: SETT → CTRL assigns PAGE or VOL: change pattern pages or adjust the current row’s volume. This is the same knob accepting two quite different explanations of what you wanted more of.
sequencing.html.sequencing.015: Mute/unmute the current voice; the notes stay stored. See Advanced → Mutes. A voice can be asked to wait without being asked to forget its part.
sequencing.html.sequencing.017: Hold to solo the voice. While held, encoder 3 changes fast filter and encoder 4 chooses a random sample. Release to return. See Advanced → Mutes.
sequencing.html.sequencing.019: Adjust this channel’s default filter-page parameter. Having chosen the thing you reach for most, you may now reach it without a journey through the editor.
sequencing.html.sequencing.021: Start/pause the sequencer. The next press resumes the conversation with time.
sequencing.html.sequencing.023: Open the focused voice’s filter editor where its channel supports FX. A useful place to go when the timing is right and the sound is having other difficulties.
sequencing.html.sequencing.025: Move the cursor across steps 1…32. Choose the instant first; the event can follow.
sequencing.html.sequencing.027: Places a note in an empty cell. It can also replace an inaudible lower note already covered by a higher note of the same monophonic voice at that step.
sequencing.html.sequencing.029: On an empty cell, hold and turn to paint a trail. On an existing note, open its per-step editor. The difference between an empty and occupied starting cell is substantial; inspect it before holding.
sequencing.html.sequencing.030: Single — allowing a small problem to remain small
sequencing.html.sequencing.031: There is a stage in composition when every part seems to require attention, generally just after you add the part intended to make everything simpler. Single mode helps by bringing the chosen voice to full intensity while the others fade to their base colours. The rest of the arrangement is still there. It has ceased waving at you. Now a bassline can be considered as a bassline, rather than as one of several reasons the whole piece seems to lean slightly to the left. Edit one voice, hear it in context, and give yourself a chance to finish a thought.
sequencing.html.sequencing.032: Single mode: the focused voice is bright white and other voices use dim base colours. Shadowed, inaudible notes use 20% of their normal brightness.
sequencing.html.sequencing.033: From draw, choose voice 1–8, 11, 13 or 14 and tap L (touch 1). Tap again to return. You cannot enter from row 16 or empty voices 9, 10 and 12. Once in single, row 16 is available for page tools. Draw gestures still work, with a narrower scope: copy/paste takes the focused channel, the encoder 1 + encoder 4 long chord clears that channel on the current edit page, and page-row randomize fills that channel. Narrower scope is a considerable comfort when experimenting. You may be entirely wrong about the bass without requiring the snare to start its life over.
sequencing.html.sequencing.034: A brief theory of making a note exist
sequencing.html.sequencing.035: A lit step is a trigger: play this voice at this instant. This modest instruction does a great deal of work. It says nothing about whether the noise is tasteful, whether the audience is ready, or whether you ought to have gone to bed. It simply makes the noise happen at the requested time. Placing a trigger is called paint; removing one is unpaint. SETT → DRAW decides which encoders do those jobs. There are two arrangements, chiefly distinguished by how many hands you would like to involve.
sequencing.html.sequencing.036: L+R and R — practical theories of hand ownership
sequencing.html.sequencing.037: In L+R, writing and erasing have separate knobs: right hand creates, left hand revises. It is a remarkably compact model of the creative process. In R, encoder 4 handles both jobs, leaving encoder 1 available for a performance break. The grid and stored notes are the same in either case. Choose according to your hands and the circumstances in which you expect to use them. A perfectly good arrangement at a desk can become inconvenient when one hand is occupied elsewhere.
sequencing.html.sequencing.039: Two hands: left on encoder 1, right on encoder 4.
sequencing.html.sequencing.040: One hand can do most writing and erasing on encoder 4.
sequencing.html.sequencing.042: Short-press encoder 4 to place a trigger; hold and turn for a painted trail.
sequencing.html.sequencing.043: Short-press encoder 4 on empty to place; hold and turn to paint.
sequencing.html.sequencing.045: Short-press encoder 1 to erase; hold and turn for an erased trail.
sequencing.html.sequencing.046: Short-press encoder 4 on a trigger to remove; hold and turn to erase.
sequencing.html.sequencing.048: Turn encoder 1 to choose the voice.
sequencing.html.sequencing.049: Turn encoder 1 to choose the voice. Its address-book duties survive the reorganisation.
sequencing.html.sequencing.051: Erase the cursor’s note. A local edit.
sequencing.html.sequencing.052: Temporary full mute for a performance break. A silence with several possible ways out.
sequencing.html.sequencing.054: Careful editing: one hand chooses the voice while the other chooses time.
sequencing.html.sequencing.055: One-hand live drawing, with quick performance breaks available.
sequencing.html.sequencing.056: Change the method under SETT → DRAW whenever useful. The pattern stays as it is. You are rearranging the working tools, much as somebody might move a pen to their other hand without expecting the letter already written to change its contents.
sequencing.html.sequencing.057: L+R paint — an agreement between the hands
sequencing.html.sequencing.058: The left hand chooses who; the right chooses when and presses to commit. A rhythm can emerge quite naturally from moving between these two questions. Begin with one voice and a few events. There is no entrance examination requiring a complicated pattern, though many musicians spend their first hour behaving as if an examiner might be concealed in the headphones.
sequencing.html.sequencing.059: Turn encoder 1 to select the voice row. Choose who gets the next event.
sequencing.html.sequencing.060: Turn encoder 4 to choose its step in time. Leave space where you want space; empty cells are doing work too.
sequencing.html.sequencing.061: Tap encoder 4 to place a trigger at the cursor. It will sound when the playhead next reaches it.
sequencing.html.sequencing.062: Hold encoder 4 and turn to paint a continuous trail of triggers. Several future moments have now been given the same task.
sequencing.html.sequencing.063: L+R: encoder 1 selects the lane; encoder 4 moves through time and writes. A simple division of labour, shown before the hands develop artistic differences.
sequencing.html.sequencing.064: L+R unpaint — a useful form of second thought
sequencing.html.sequencing.065: Encoder 1 removes what encoder 4 placed. Its work is just as important. A dense pattern can be made more interesting by taking one event out, an economy which can feel suspicious after spending so long acquiring equipment. Try the gap while playback runs. A note that seemed indispensable may turn out to have been covering a much better silence.
sequencing.html.sequencing.066: Tap encoder 1 to erase the trigger beneath the cursor.
sequencing.html.sequencing.067: Hold encoder 1 and turn to erase a trail. Check where you begin and how far you intend to go.
sequencing.html.sequencing.068: In L+R, encoder 4 writes and encoder 1 erases. Neither toggles between the two jobs. Your right hand can be enthusiastic and your left hand selective, without requiring either to decide what kind of hand it is on every press.
sequencing.html.sequencing.070: Choose DRAW = R and encoder 4 writes or erases according to what it finds. Short-press an empty cell to place a trigger; short-press a lit cell to remove it. For held trails, the starting cell decides the operation: start empty to paint, occupied to erase. That decision remains in force throughout the gesture. It would be inconvenient if the knob reconsidered its purpose at every cell, and much like trying to decorate a room with a brush which occasionally decided it was a sponge.
sequencing.html.sequencing.071: Tap encoder 4 to toggle the cell: empty becomes a trigger; a trigger becomes empty.
sequencing.html.sequencing.072: Hold encoder 4 and turn. An empty starting cell paints the trail; a trigger at the start makes it erase. Inspect the first cell.
sequencing.html.sequencing.073: Turn encoder 1 to select the voice row. Only its erasing duty has moved.
sequencing.html.sequencing.074: R: encoder 4 writes and erases. Encoder 1 still chooses voices, and its press has acquired the larger subject of silence.
sequencing.html.sequencing.075: The performance break — the importance of the next sound
sequencing.html.sequencing.076: In R mode, press encoder 1 for a temporary full mute. Everything goes quiet, but the notes remain. A well-placed silence can make a room attend more closely than another layer of percussion; it also gives the musician a brief opportunity to look as though this was planned all along. Leaving the break determines which voices come back. Choose the return with one of the four encoder presses below. The silence is temporary. Its dramatic interpretation is yours.
sequencing.html.sequencing.077: Encoder 1 again: restore the mute states from before the break. Resume the previous cast, with the benefit of a short absence.
sequencing.html.sequencing.078: Encoder 2: unmute only channels 1 and 2. Two voices can make a surprisingly large entrance when they have the room to themselves.
sequencing.html.sequencing.079: Encoder 3: use the custom return set from SETT → MUTE. Prepare who returns, then enjoy appearing spontaneous.
sequencing.html.sequencing.080: Encoder 4: unmute everything. The whole cast arrives together. Leave them some headroom.
sequencing.html.sequencing.081: SETT → MUTE defines the custom set brought back by encoder 3. It does not limit which rows you can paint. For example, prepare a kick-and-snare return: after the full mute, one press brings those two back while the other voices stay muted. A familiar rhythm is briefly heard with more space around it. You have changed the listener’s attention without writing another note, a useful discovery when the pattern was already quite full.
sequencing.html.sequencing.082: A performance break keeps the notes; clearing removes them. For strip deletion, move to the page row and, in L+R, unpaint the page LED with encoder 1; see Pages+More → Delete a page. The encoder 1 + encoder 4 long chord or single-mode clear operates on the current edit page. These are deletion commands, with different scopes. A break is expecting the music to return. Choose a clear operation only when you intend to remove its notes.

pages-more.html.pages-more.001: A short history of wanting another page
pages-more.html.pages-more.002: At first, one page is an enormous amount of space. You can put a kick here, a snare there, and still have room for several errors of judgement. Then you write something you like. Immediately it becomes necessary to have a second page in which almost the same thing happens, but with a slightly different hi-hat. This innocent requirement is how arrangements begin. Row 16 provides the extra territory and the means of moving, copying and clearing it. The more elaborate consequences are discussed in Advanced Sequencing.
pages-more.html.pages-more.004: Move encoder 1 to the very top, row 16 (y==16). The dots are your 8 pattern pages. Each looks reassuringly small. This is misleading: a page dot represents a whole stretch of music, much as a modest dot on a map can represent a town containing a station, three supermarkets and somebody who is absolutely certain you have parked in their space. From here, your gestures operate on that larger thing.
pages-more.html.pages-more.005: The cursor must be on row 16. That is the condition for delete page, copy/paste, clear, random fill and note-shift. On a voice row (y ≠ 16), the same buttons paint, erase, mute or do nothing. This is worth checking before pressing the button several more times. Increasing the frequency of a wrong instruction has never made a computer understand the right one, though it has kept generations of computer owners very busy.
pages-more.html.pages-more.006: The bottom hints and encoder rings change colour when the cursor reaches the page row. Think of this as the instrument looking up from its desk and saying, “A whole page? Are we doing whole pages now?” Ordinary draw/single colours mean that it has not yet been informed of the expansion.
pages-more.html.pages-more.007: Having reached the top, you may now make the following substantially larger decisions:
pages-more.html.pages-more.008: Delete a page by unpainting its strip LED. This removes notes, rather than merely making the little light less obtrusive.
pages-more.html.pages-more.009: Copy and paste the page. Draw takes all voices; single takes the focused voice. The hi-hat variation that started this whole business is now within reach.
pages-more.html.pages-more.010: Clear the current edit page with encoder 1 long on the page row: all voices in draw, the focused voice in single.
pages-more.html.pages-more.012: Note-shift moves the focused voice in time or across rows, in single mode. It is the instrument’s answer to the very human conviction that the notes would be excellent if only they were somewhere else.
pages-more.html.pages-more.014: The page LEDs report occupancy using hasNotes. They can tell you whether something is there. They cannot tell you whether it ought to be there. This limitation has proved beneficial to relations between the instrument and its owner.
pages-more.html.pages-more.021: The demolition of a very small dot
pages-more.html.pages-more.022: There is a moment in almost every creative project when its author decides that one section is beyond saving. Occasionally this is sound judgement. Occasionally the author needs lunch. The instrument cannot distinguish these conditions. On the page row, unpaint clears the entire page beneath the cursor. A dark-blue occupied page becomes empty, and the machine assumes that this was what you meant.
pages-more.html.pages-more.023: Put the cursor on row 16. Check the changed hint colours. You are about to act on a page, so it is useful to be on one.
pages-more.html.pages-more.024: With encoder 4, choose the page LED you intend to clear. Dark blue means it has notes. Consider them briefly.
pages-more.html.pages-more.025: In DRAW = L+R, press encoder 1 on that strip LED. This is the operative part of the decision; everything before it was merely looking determined.
pages-more.html.pages-more.027: In draw, all voices across that page’s 32 steps are cleared. Every instrument on the page receives the same short notice.
pages-more.html.pages-more.028: In single, only the focused voice is cleared. Other voices remain, and the page stays occupied until all of them are empty. A bassline cannot declare a page vacant while a perfectly serviceable snare is still living there.
pages-more.html.pages-more.029: A fully empty page turns very dark red. The playback range, lastPage, also updates, removing trailing empty pages from the journey. The machine is therefore prepared to stop visiting a place once you have removed everything worth visiting. Many transport authorities could learn from this.
pages-more.html.pages-more.030: R mode has a different arrangement. Encoder 4 on the page strip performs copy/paste. For strip erasing, use L+R or the clear-page gestures below. Copying a passage you were trying to remove is an especially efficient way to discover how much you disliked it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.031: There is no undo. Save the page to PATT before clearing it if you might want it back. The future has a habit of becoming rather sentimental about things the present found intolerable.
pages-more.html.pages-more.032: A short press on the page row does nothing. Encoder 1 long deletes the current edit page: all voices in draw, the focused voice in single. Random fill waits for FN + encoder 2 long. The machine will not invent a part merely because you tapped too quickly.
pages-more.html.pages-more.034: Row 1 has four cues, one above each encoder, repeated by the rings. They are a compact substitute for having a tiny person beside each knob explain its present responsibilities. The tiny people were considered impractical, and would almost certainly have formed opinions about the music.
pages-more.html.pages-more.056: On the page row in draw, encoder 1 is red and encoder 4 yellow. Page dots continue to show content, and the cursor marks the target. These lights remain admirably factual during moments when the musician’s intentions have become largely emotional.
pages-more.html.pages-more.057: Red over encoder 1, yellow over encoder 4. You have the larger tools out.
pages-more.html.pages-more.061: Does nothing on the page row. While a copy is armed, this short press cancels it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.063: Wipes every voice on the current edit page. No undo; check the destination before demolishing it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.071: In single mode, open the focused voice’s filters. In draw, the page row maps to channel 15, which has no filter path. There is nothing there to make warmer.
pages-more.html.pages-more.073: Move across steps and pages; the edit page follows the cursor’s position. You are choosing where the next operation will land.
pages-more.html.pages-more.075: First tap: copy the current edit page, all voices. Second tap: paste onto the page you have reached. See Advanced → Copy & paste. Music can now repeat without requiring you to repeat yourself.
pages-more.html.pages-more.077: The first encoder 4 tap leaves encoder 1 blue (cancel) and turns encoder 4 green (paste), with c+p in yellow at the centre. The parcel is now visible, which is the least the buffer can do. Continue with Advanced Sequencing → Copy & paste. FN + touch 2 copies and pastes the same way.
pages-more.html.pages-more.078: Single, with room for one more good idea
pages-more.html.pages-more.079: Single uses red, white and yellow hints on encoders 1, 2 and 4. The copy contains only the focused voice. You can copy the hi-hat, change focus, and paste onto a different voice. The new voice receives the rhythm without receiving any explanation of why the hi-hat thought it appropriate. This is, in miniature, how musical traditions spread.
pages-more.html.pages-more.080: Single’s red, white and yellow hints. The rest of the band is safe from this particular experiment.
pages-more.html.pages-more.082: Does nothing on the page row. While a copy is armed, this short press cancels it. The other voices remain unconsulted.
pages-more.html.pages-more.084: Deletes every note of the focused voice on the current edit page. No undo. A fresh pattern is FN + encoder 2 long. See Advanced → Random.
pages-more.html.pages-more.094: First tap copies the focused voice; second tap pastes onto the voice currently in focus. See Advanced → Copy & paste.
pages-more.html.pages-more.095: Clear and randomize cannot be undone. The last PATT save is your way back. If the page was never saved, the handbook can offer sympathy, but it would be dishonest of it to describe sympathy as a recovery procedure.

advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.001: Some experiments in making the music behave differently
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.002: A groove is a small community of noises that have reached a temporary understanding. Advanced sequencing lets you test the understanding. You can silence one member, move another, duplicate the entire gathering, or invite a machine to suggest what is missing. The community may improve. It may also become so interesting that you reload the old pattern. Page-row geography is in Pages+More; the ordinary means of making notes are in Sequencing.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.004: Most of these tools require row 16, y==16, usually in single mode. Mutes need a voice row. Row 1 indicates which tool is armed; consult Pages+More for the colours. A naturalist searching for a particular creature begins by finding its habitat. The same principle applies to note-shift, although note-shift is considerably less likely to bite.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.006: One of the quickest ways to improve a piece of music is to stop part of it. This is an awkward discovery, and musicians have developed elaborate vocabulary to avoid making it sound personal. On a voice row, hold encoder 2 for the temporary mute/solo overlay. The other lanes mute, leaving the current voice alone. Release to restore them. A short press toggles the lane’s mute persistently. Nothing is erased. The noises have been asked to wait outside, rather than informed that the species is extinct.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.007: Muted lanes dim. Active lanes remain bright. The silence is represented without requiring a blank display.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.008: While encoder 2 is held, you can examine the surviving voice more closely:
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.009: Encoder 3, green: the current voice’s fast filter. An isolated sound can now be persuaded to become less obviously the reason you isolated it.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.010: Encoder 4, pink: browse the random sample playlist, ?> / ?<, and short-press to load the last preview. This is rather like asking whether the drummer could improve the groove and being offered a waterfall. Try it before dismissing it.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.012: On row 16, encoder 2 short enters note-shift in single mode. To mute, return to a voice row. The machinery distinguishes the removal of a sound from the relocation of its notes even when its operator is still deciding.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.013: R mode’s temporary full mute is a separate arrangement on encoder 1. Its return options are in Sequencing → R mode and SETT → MUTE. There are surprisingly many varieties of silence. Most become distinguishable at the moment they end.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.015: Imagine discovering that an animal’s entire migratory route was one step too far to the left. A large research grant would be needed to move the landscape. Note-shift is cheaper: it moves actual step data through time and across rows. Moving rows is the grid’s transpose operation; there is no separate global transpose page. If you want to change the pitch while leaving the written steps alone, use detune and octave in Sound design. This distinction matters chiefly when you later look for the notes where you left them.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.016: In single mode on row 16, short-press the white encoder 2. Other voices are snapshotted while the focused one becomes movable. Encoder 1 glows bright green, encoder 4 bright blue, and a grey marquee crosses row 1. It is a reassuring quantity of visible preparation for what can otherwise look alarmingly like the notes deciding to leave.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.018: Shift the focused voice vertically across the whole pattern. Notes wrap at the edges. The world is round in this rather specialised direction.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.027: The white page-row cue is the sign for note-shift. Encoder 2 short on a voice row will not enter it. Check the habitat before concluding the creature has disappeared.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.029: On the page row, short-press encoder 4 to copy. Draw takes all voices on the edit page; single takes only the focused voice and can paste it into another voice after a focus change. An exact repetition may be described as structure or as a lack of ideas. The machine wisely leaves that decision to the reviews.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.031: The first tap stores the copy, leaves encoder 1 blue to cancel, turns encoder 4 green to paste, and shows c+p in yellow at the centre. Navigate to the destination, then tap encoder 4 again to paste. Encoder 1 short cancels. FN + touch 2 does the same copy and paste. This is a useful moment to remember whether you wanted the phrase here, there, or merely somewhere that would make it easier to think about.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.032: Copy armed: page strip cleared, blue cancel and green paste cues. The yellow c+p label confirms that a copy is waiting.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.034: First tap: fill the buffer. Second tap: paste onto the current page and, in single, the current voice. Confirm where you are before making there more like here.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.036: Page row, hold FN, long-press encoder 2. That is the only in-grid randomize: the focused voice in single, a multi-voice page in draw. Encoder 1 long on that row deletes instead. The distinction is particularly worth checking when your plan is to let the machine contribute, since deleting your contribution first can give it an exaggerated sense of its importance.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.037: The companion replaces only the focused voice on the current edit page. It studies the other voices across the active pattern, giving the current and neighbouring pages extra weight, and responds to accents, velocities and tonal centre. In other words, it listens before joining in. This is such a promising innovation in musical collaboration that one is tempted to make it compulsory. It assumes the following roles for the channels:
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.041: Kick and snare retain rhythmic anchors, though the snare may arrive a step early or late in response to kick, clap and ensemble density. Hats, claps and toms explore sparse Euclidean patterns with different pulse counts and full 16-step rotations; claps can reinforce a snare or fill a vacant backbeat. On 32-step pages the second half gets a related rotation. Every role may use different pitch rows. Bass responds to kick, existing bass and harmony, preferring root and fifth. Bass, keys and pads share a page-level key, scale and four-slot progression, such as minor i–VI–III–VII. Sample keys and pads stay monophonic; synth lanes 13 and 14 take one tone each of a two-note chord. Channels 1–8 never receive stacked chords. Channel 11 permits three voices, though its bass role normally writes one note. Choices weight approximately 60% chord tones, 30% other scale tones and 10% chromatic passing notes. That last ten per cent is where a computer briefly looks as though it has had an interesting childhood. Faster tempos thin the decorations. With no other voices to study, it invents a varied 4/4 starting point. Long-press again for another reading of the evidence.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.042: Clear and randomize have no undo. Recover from the last PATT save. The companion will listen, suggest and try again, but remains entirely incapable of remembering the particular unsaved version you have just decided was perfect.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.043: For a larger experiment, use MODE → AUTO. It studies the orange base-page range and writes coordinated variations into the following green pages. An empty base creates a complete starter ensemble. The astonishing thing is less that it can develop your ideas than that it will make this effort even when you have supplied no ideas at all.

samples.html.samples.002: There are sounds which people travel great distances to hear, and sounds which cause people to move house. A sampler is admirably free of prejudice about the distinction. Both become data. The sample browser is where you find a recorded noise, trim its less promising extremities, and decide whether it deserves one of voices 1–8.
samples.html.samples.004: Before entering the undergrowth, settle the size of the expedition. KIT replaces the samples for all eight voices, as explained in Sample kits. SMP changes one current voice, channel 1–8, using a file under samples/. SMP provides trim, reverse, preview and load. It is entirely possible to spend an agreeable evening selecting a single snare. The instrument imposes no upper limit on this activity, and cannot be held responsible for what happens to the evening.
samples.html.samples.005: The noise must be a mono 16-bit WAV at 44.1 kHz, at most 12 seconds per voice. These conditions apply regardless of the sound’s rarity, emotional significance or resemblance to a dying refrigerator. The SD card chapter explains how to get it aboard.
